body.text: Few places or corridors tell a richer story of geography and human movement than J. M. W. Turner. Stepping into its history reveals how trade, terrain, and culture shaped the modern map.

Joseph Mallord William Turner (23 April 1775, 19 December 1851), known during his lifetime as William Turner, was an English Romantic painter who is regarded as one of the greatest British painters of the 19th century.
His expressive renditions of light and atmosphere and bold use of colour in landscape painting inspired the early impressionist painters Claude Monet and Camille Pissarro.

Turner started his career as an architectural draughtsman and watercolourist and gained academic recognition as an oil painter. A child prodigy, he was accepted as a student at the Royal Academy of Arts at the age of 14 and quickly rose to fame and financial success.

By his early twenties he was selling oil paintings at top market prices and gaining high praise from the academic establishment. By 27 he was a Royal Academician, the highest artistic honour at the time. He was one of the youngest painters to achieve this distinction in the Academy's history.
Despite these accomplishments, a few influential critics in aristocratic circles constantly criticised him for his working-class origins.

Turner's artistic style evolved during his lifetime as he never stopped experimenting with new painting techniques. He was a versatile artist who could emulate the styles of Old Masters, producing works that earned admiration from Academicians and art critics.

Early on, he started painting in an increasingly expressionistic style, using sketches from his extensive travels throughout England and Europe as inspiration. To complement his depictions of the ocean, rivers and mountains, he experimented with representing natural phenomena like sunlight, storms, clouds and fog.

Turner's later landscapes became more abstract and were not well received at the time, but are today considered masterpieces. He was a prolific artist, producing about 550 oil paintings and over 2,000 watercolours during his lifetime.

Turner died a rich man in 1851, at the age of 76. Upon his death, his investments and properties were valued at £140,000 (equivalent to £17 million in 2025). He bequeathed to the nation around 100 finished and 200 unfinished oil paintings.
His most important works are displayed at the National Gallery and the Tate Britain museums in London.
Biography
Childhood

Turner was born on 23 April 1775 in a house on Maiden Lane, a street in London's working-class Covent Garden district, during the day it was a thriving commercial market and a busy area at night due to its concentration of theatres, taverns and brothels.

The family moved to Hand Court, on the other side from Maiden Lane, when Turner was five years old. Turner was sent to different towns to attend elementary school, including Brentford, Margate and Sunningwell (now part of Oxfordshire).

Turner's father, William Turner, had a barbershop and wig store on the first floor. By the time Turner was ten years old, he proudly displayed his young son's drawings in the window, which he let customers view up close for one shilling.
His father boasted to the artist Thomas Stothard: "My son, sir, is going to be a painter". He would later retire as a barber to help his son in various tasks in his studio and paint gallery.

His mother, Mary Marshall, came from a family of butchers. She started to show symptoms of mental disorder and as they got worse, Turner's father was forced to place her in St Luke's Hospital for Lunatics. She was later moved to Bethlem Hospital, a mental asylum commonly known as "Bedlam", where she died in 1804.
Adult life

The inspiration Turner found in the river Thames motivated him to occupy several second homes on or very near the river. The river allowed him to relax by fishing and boating, two of his favourite activities.

He rented houses in Isleworth (1804, 1806) and Hammersmith, where he converted a boat into a floating studio (1807, 1811). In 1811 he bought a plot of land in Twickenham, where he built a house he named Sandycombe Lodge.

Old age

Turner's appearance in his later years disconcerted those who met him, as it was difficult to imagine how such an unprepossessing man could produce paintings of such beauty. Observers reported he reminded them of "an English farmer", a "long-stage coachman" or a "river-boat sailor", rather than a renowned painter.
When he was young, he invested in fine clothes in order to fit into academic circles, but in his fifties, following his father's death, he became careless about his appearance.

In his seventies, Turner formed a relationship with the widow Sophia Caroline Booth. He frequently stayed with her under the pseudonym "Mr Booth" or "Admiral Booth", in her house at 6 Davis's Place (now Cheyne Walk) in Chelsea, London. He died at the house on 19 December 1851, at the age of 76.
Bequest

In an unprecedented gesture, Turner bequeathed to the nation about 100 finished oil paintings as well as 200 unfinished canvases, over 19,000 sketches, drawings and watercolours and some 200 sketchbooks.
The finished oil paintings were worth a small fortune, considering that they had been regularly purchased for no less than 200 guineas and up to 450 guineas during his lifetime.
In 1856, after five years of legal disputes started by his cousins, his financial assets were divided among the family, and the Academy received £20,000.

Turner specified that a new gallery should house the bequeathed paintings. At the time, this did not happen because they disagreed over the final site. In 1987, Tate Britain inaugurated the Clore Gallery, fulfilling his final wishes 136 years after his death.
Career
Early commercial work

While still a young man, he secured a reliable income thanks to the rising demand for topographical and architectural watercolours. He worked for several architects, including Thomas Hardwick, James Wyatt and Joseph Bonomi the Elder. In 1789 he began to study under the topographical draughtsman Thomas Malton, who specialised in London views.
The Academy

Turner was recognised as a child prodigy and accepted into the Royal Academy Schools in 1789, at the age of 14, where he was an accomplished student and made rapid progress. Only a year after starting his studies, the watercolour A View of the Archbishop's Palace, Lambeth was accepted to the Academy's Annual Exhibition.
In 1796, the Academy awarded the 18-year-old the Greater Silver Palette award for landscape drawing.

At 21, he exhibited the oil painting Fishermen at Sea, a dramatic moonlit seascape. The work drew widespread acclaim from contemporary critics and established Turner's reputation as a promising talent in marine painting. During his years at the Academy, Turner was keenly focused on obtaining academic recognition.

He followed the teachings of Sir Joshua Reynolds, which at the time defined the Academy's criteria for judging artistic excellence. Reynolds advocated the study and emulation of the Old Masters, in particular those from Italy, Spain and the Netherlands.

Dutch Boats in a Gale copied the style of 17th-century Dutch marine painters and was presented the following year at the Royal Academy Exhibition of 1801 and "took the Academy by storm". It was hung in the best location of the whole exhibition: in the Great Room, centred, and opposite to the entrance.

It so impressed the Academy and the art critics that the following year Turner was admitted as a Royal Academician. At only 27 years of age, he became the second youngest artist in the institution's history to achieve the highest artistic academic recognition in England.
Commercial success
" During his sketching excursions, he was always searching for visual ideas but also on the lookout for saleable subjects.

Even though the Napoleonic Wars had considerably reduced the demand for large historical paintings, Turner kept selling them at top prices and receiving substantial commissions from wealthy patrons, which disconcerted older members of the Academy. He took advantage of the demand for pendants, works that were commissioned to hang next to an existing painting.
